newsitem.title: USA: Clinton holds "dress rehearsals" for Dole debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton holds "dress rehearsals" for Dole debate.

text.p: By a secluded lake set in a blaze of autumnal trees, President Bill Clinton will spent the next two days essentially play acting as he prepares for Sunday's debate with Republican Bob Dole.

With a former senator playing Dole, a host of handlers scripting his every word and a drama school graduate steeped in Shakespeare coaching him, Clinton plans to hold "dress rehearsals" each night to ready himself for the encounter.
Nationally broadcast debates -- a central feature of U.S. politics since John Kennedy squared off in 1960 against Richard Nixon -- are too important for anything to be left to chance.

As a result, Clinton has abandoned the campaign trail, the White House and his wife and daughter for three days to isolate himself in this remote corner of New York state to prepare for the first of two face-to-face meetings with Dole.
The men were scheduled to debate each other at 9 p.m. Sunday (0100 GMT on Monday) in Hartford, Conn. and then again on Wednesday, Oct. 16, in San Diego.
In between, Vice President Al Gore and Dole runningmate Jack Kemp are to meet on Wednesday Oct. 9.
One measure of the debates' importance was in the lengthy cast of characters assembled to prepare Clinton.
Former Maine Sen. George Mitchell, a Democrat who like Dole once served as the Senate majority leader, will pretend to be the Republican candidate in the daily debate practice.

All the president's top political men, including senior adviser George Stephanopoulos, chief of staff Leon Panetta and his deputy Harold Ickes, have come to this 750-acre retreat to help the president hone his performance.
And Michael Sheehan, a graduate of the Yale Drama School who once worked at Washington's Folger Theater, which specializes in performing Shakespeare, will be on hand to advise the president.

Clinton, whose normal campaign schedule often begins shortly after dawn and ends past midnight, arrived in Chautauqua on Thursday afternoon and has not a single public event scheduled until he leaves for Hartford on Sunday.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters the president planned to take most of Thursday afternoon off and then to throw himself into his debate practice.

"We plan to do one dress rehearsal each evening at roughly the same time that the debate will happen -- between 9 p.m. nad 10:30 p.m. -- to get the body clock oriented in the right direction," McCurry added.

While Clinton was expected to spend most waking hours cramming for the debate, aides said he was likely to take some time to hike, jog or play golf, saying one of their aims was for him to be as rested and relaxed as possible.
Chautauqua, a gated, Victorian resort, was in the early stages of autumn, with the leaves on its trees gradually turning red, russet and gold as the cold weather sets in.
Dole has also been devoting himself to debate preparation for much of the past week, surrounded by top aides in the sunny Florida resort of Bar Harbour.

Trailing Clinton by anywhere from 10 to 20 percentage points in national opinion polls, the debates would appear to be Dole's best chance to take his case directly to the electorate and to argue he would make a better president.
